summary.text: Wave optics, also called physical optics, studies interference, diffraction and polarization, which the simple straight-ray picture of light cannot explain.
The name also covers an approximation that uses rays to estimate the field at a surface, then adds up that field across the surface to find the transmitted or scattered light.
It sits between ray optics, which ignores waves, and full wave electromagnetism, and it is a standard way to estimate diffraction effects.

facts.label: Middle ground
facts.value: Between geometric optics and full wave electromagnetism

facts.label: Weak spot
facts.value: Inaccurate near edges and shadow boundaries

facts.label: Works best on
facts.value: Large smooth convex shapes and low-reflection surfaces

facts.label: Improved theory
facts.value: A 2004 version gives exact answers for diffraction by conducting scatterers

items.prompt: An engineer uses the same approximation for a light beam and a radio signal. Why does it usually fit the light beam better?

options.label: Light has a much higher frequency, and the method suits high frequencies
Light waves are longer, so they bend around objects more gently
Radio waves get absorbed by air before anyone can measure them
Light has no wave behavior, so rays fit it exactly every time

items.explain: Physical optics is a high-frequency approximation, so it tends to be more accurate for optical light than for radio.

items.prompt: A photographer sees faint fringes around a tiny hole that straight-line rays would not predict. Which branch deals with this?

options.label: Geometric optics, since straight lines describe it fully
Coherence theory, which is about quantum noise in communication
Wave optics, because rays fail for effects like this
Ray optics with a stronger lens fitted to the camera

items.explain: Wave optics covers phenomena where the ray approximation of geometric optics is not valid, such as diffraction.

items.prompt: You trust ray-based estimates across a big smooth mirror, then try the same trick right at a sharp shadow edge. What happens?

options.label: It works equally well at the edge as in the middle
It loses accuracy unless diffraction corrections are added
It fails everywhere because rays never apply to mirrors
It gets more accurate because the light is concentrated

items.explain: The ray-based field is generally not accurate near edges or shadow boundaries unless supplemented with diffraction calculations.

items.prompt: How does the approximation find the light that comes through a lens?

options.label: It solves the full electromagnetic equations at every point inside the glass
It adds up the colors of the rays reaching the focus
It ignores the lens and treats the light as one straight ray
It estimates the field with rays, then integrates that field over the lens

items.explain: In optics it typically integrates a ray-estimated field over a lens, mirror or aperture to get the transmitted or scattered field.

items.prompt: A radar wave hits a ship. When the approximation is applied, how is the hidden far side of the ship treated?

options.label: It carries the same current as the lit front
It is assumed to carry no current
It carries half the current of the front
It is solved exactly with a separate full theory

items.explain: Current on the shadowed parts is taken as zero, and only the geometrically illuminated front is used.

items.prompt: A student says the first word in 'physical optics' means it is the exact true theory of light. What is the correction?

options.label: It only means the method models more wave effects than ray optics; it is not exact
It means the method applies only to solid physical objects
It means the method was proven by experiment to be exact
It means the method measures physical forces on light

items.explain: The word means it is more physical than ray optics, not that it is an exact physical theory.
